newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Pensions, reform high on Japan PM's agenda in NZ.
newsitem.headline: Pensions, reform high on Japan PM's agenda in NZ.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto will discuss ways of tackling the social costs of an ageing population with his New Zealand counterpart Jim Bolger during a visit this week, officials said on Tuesday.
Hashimoto is due in Wellington late on Tuesday night for the last leg of a three-day Australasian tour.
Foreign ministry officials said the visit would give the two leaders "the opportunity to exchange ideas on domestic reform", which they noted was a hot issue in Japan.
Bolger told parliament he expected the focus of the talks to include "social policy, where both countries are facing the implications for retirement incomes policy for an ageing society".
Hashimoto is publicly committed to six areas of reform, including deregulating the economy and scaling down government.
But many commentators doubt his administration will be able to turn much of that agenda into reality.
At the same time, Japan faces a crisis from the rapid ageing of its population that means its current funding structures for healthcare will be unable to cope with forecast demands.

New Zealand, which went through two phases of radical reform in the early 1980s and 1990s that helped unwind a virtual command economy and deregulate almost all markets, has studied such problems extensively and wants to replace old schemes soon.
The coalition government has put a lot of its political energy since its was formed in December into trying to find a good model for a possible new private pension scheme.

Officials suggested Hashimoto would take a keen interest in this area. A meeting with Treasurer Winston Peters, the champion of the so-called "compulsory super" plan, is among his handful of engagements on Wednesday.

Other issues on the bilateral agenda will include representations from New Zealand on environmental issues. Lobbyists are keen to have opposition to Japan's role in nuclear waste shipments and whaling aired.
Bolger told parliament he was prepared to raise environmental subjects even if the nations disagreed on them.
"Our relationship is sufficiently mature to have constructive exchanges on areas where there are differences of opinion," he said.
